title: Judge "Highly Likely" To Grant Apple Injunction As OpenAI Fires Back With Its Own Theft Allegations
desc:
Judge "Highly Likely" To Grant Apple Injunction As OpenAI Fires Back With Its Own Theft Allegations

The judge overseeing Apple's trade-secret case against OpenAI said Wednesday he is "highly likely" to grant an injunction barring use of the iPhone maker's proprietary information, a potential setback for the ChatGPT maker's push into consumer hardware, Bloomberg reports.

Ahead of the hearing, however, OpenAI delivered its own accusation: a former employee allegedly took confidential files about an unreleased OpenAI device before returning to Apple, then presented OpenAI's product plans to senior Apple executives. Apple says it found no evidence to substantiate the claims.

The companies that partnered two years ago to bring ChatGPT into Apple's software are now accusing each other of benefiting from the transfer of confidential hardware information. Apparently, the partnership did not include sharing the blueprints.

A Few Bad Apples

Speaking at Wednesday's hearing in San Jose, US District Judge Edward Davila signaled that Apple would likely receive an order preventing use of its proprietary information. But he was less enthusiastic about the company's request for a forensic inspection of all devices and repositories containing Apple trade secrets, describing it as a "huge ask," according to Bloomberg.

Apple attorney John M. Desmarais responded that the company would narrow its inspections to a limited group of former employees now at OpenAI.

"They don't have 400 bad apples, your honor, they have a few bad apples and know who they are," Desmarais said.

The distinction matters: Davila signaled likely preliminary relief, not a final judgment that OpenAI stole Apple's technology. His reported comments also did not amount to an order shutting down OpenAI's hardware program. The practical impact would depend on the terms of an actual injunction.

Apple sued OpenAI, hardware chief Tang Yew Tan and former iPhone engineer Chang Liu in July, alleging a scheme to obtain confidential information covering product design, manufacturing, component technologies, testing methods and its supply chain. Apple says that information is being used to help OpenAI enter the consumer hardware market.

OpenAI denies the allegations and argues that Apple is trying to restrain employees from joining a competitor, portraying "ordinary job interviews" as acts of trade secret misappropriation.

"OpenAI is developing a new family of devices designed for the AI era," the company said in an October court filing quoted by Bloomberg. "OpenAI has no need or desire for Apple's trade secrets."

Its defense also challenges Apple's account of how former employees accessed information. In an earlier public response, OpenAI said current Apple employees had asked Liu to help locate material for their own work. It blamed Apple's account-management practices for leaving former employees with residual access and said Tan had explicitly instructed his team not to use other companies' confidential information.

Those competing explanations are now headed for closer scrutiny. According to Reuters, Davila on Tuesday allowed Apple early access to certain OpenAI digital files and approved expedited depositions of three former Apple employees, including Liu and Tan.

OpenAI Says The Files Were Moving In Both Directions

In its new court filing, OpenAI alleged that an unnamed employee joined from Apple, worked at OpenAI for six months, then returned to Apple after sending more than 100 highly confidential files to personal accounts.

The materials allegedly included images of unreleased hardware, engineering and manufacturing data, supplier information and specifications for cosmetic finishes. Some transfers occurred just after midnight in Singapore on June 2, the employee's final day at OpenAI, the filing said.

OpenAI further alleges that the employee presented its product plans to Apple's senior leadership, including its vice president of operations in Asia. The company says it is concerned that its confidential work could influence Apple's upcoming products.

The filing asks for a case schedule that would allow OpenAI to investigate and, if necessary, pursue counterclaims. It does not itself establish that Apple used the information, nor does it constitute a completed countersuit.

Apple rejected the accusations. The company said it has policies preventing employees from using confidential information belonging to former employers and found no evidence supporting OpenAI's claims, Reuters reported. Apple also accused OpenAI of trying to distract from the evidence underpinning its own lawsuit.

A Hardware Fight With Trillion-Dollar Ambitions

The dispute lands at an awkward time for OpenAI, which is targeting a $1.4 trillion valuation and preparing to go public, according to Bloomberg. Hundreds of Apple employees have moved to OpenAI, turning a software partnership into an increasingly direct contest for hardware talent and expertise.

Bloomberg has reported that OpenAI's first consumer hardware product will be a doughnut-shaped smart speaker priced above $300. People inside the company view it as a distinct, AI-centered device rather than a copy of something Apple plans to release.

But a different-looking product would not, by itself, resolve allegations about the engineering, manufacturing or supplier information used to develop it. Conversely, hiring engineers who know how to build hardware is not the same thing as stealing their former employer's files.

That is the line this case will have to establish. For OpenAI, the immediate risk is an injunction whose scope could complicate its hardware development. For Apple, the new allegations threaten to turn a case about protecting its own secrets into a dispute over how both companies handle everyone else's.

The next generation of AI devices may be revolutionary. The fight over who took what on the way out the door is decidedly old-fashioned.

title: Not 'The Onion': Harper's Magazine To Honor NPR CEO Katherine Maher With First Amendment Award

Authored by Jonathan Turley via JonathanTurley.org,

Harper's Magazine appears to be competing with The Onion in satire this week. It is awarding its First Amendment prize to NPR CEO Katherine Maher. It is akin to awarding a Second Amendment prize to Gavin Newsom. Maher has long been the very symbol of advocacy journalism and bias. Ironically, she is being given an award after steering NPR into the rocks to keep her job and its ideological bias.

Many of us have written for years about NPR's biased reporting. Not all of this criticism was made out of hostility toward the outlet - many honestly wanted NPR to reverse course and adopt more balanced coverage. That is why, when NPR was searching for a new CEO, I encouraged the board to hire a moderate figure without a history of political advocacy or controversy.

Instead, the board selected Katherine Maher, a former Wikipedia CEO widely criticized for her highly partisan and controversial public statements. She was the personification of advocacy journalism, even declaring that the First Amendment is the "number one challenge" that makes it "tricky" to censor or "modify" content as she would like.

Maher has supported "deplatforming" anyone she deems to be "fascists" and even suggested that she might support "punching Nazis." She also declared that "our reverence for the truth might be a distraction [in] getting things done."

As expected, NPR's bias only got worse. The leadership even changed a longstanding rule barring journalists from joining political protests.

One editor had had enough. Uri Berliner had watched NPR become an echo chamber for the far left with a virtual purging of all conservatives and Republicans from the newsroom. Berliner noted that NPR's Washington headquarters has 87 registered Democrats among its editors and zero Republicans.

Maher and NPR remained dismissive of such complaints. Maher attacked the award-winning Berliner for causing an "affront to the individual journalists who work incredibly hard." She called his criticism "profoundly disrespectful, hurtful, and demeaning."

Berliner resigned, after noting how Maher's "divisive views confirm the very problems at NPR" that he had been pointing out.

Rather than trying to reverse the long slide in its audience, Maher doubled down. She ultimately made the best possible case for defunding NPR. She refused to resign, effectively killing the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Yet, Harper considers her model of media.

In a press release on the awarding of the James C. Goodale First Amendment Award, Harper's declared, "As president and CEO of NPR, Katherine Maher has guided one of America's most important public media institutions through a period of extraordinary political, legal, and financial scrutiny, reaffirming journalism's essential role in a democratic society."

Maher has overseen the continued slide in ratings and revenue. In fairness, NPR's audience has been declining for years. Indeed, that trend has been most pronounced since 2017 - the period when Berliner said the company began to openly pursue a political narrative and agenda to counter Donald Trump. The falling advertising revenue has led to deep staff cuts to deal with budget shortfalls. The shrinking NPR audience remains overwhelmingly white, older, and of course liberal.

Where others see the demise of a once popular and respected outlet, Harper's sees a success story in an audience that has shed itself of conservative, libertarian, and moderate listeners - much like the audience of Harper's.

The award is the latest example of how establishment media has become a ship of fools. Journalists now report for each other as the vast majority of Americans seek alternatives. They then give each other awards and continue to replicate their own views and mistakes. The one thing that they will not do is abandon their bias.

Maher is the greatest example of why these outlets refuse to change. Despite being blamed for killing the Corporation for Public Broadcasting by refusing to resign, Maher and her staff still benefit personally from advocacy journalism. They are lionized by the left even as their influence and audience plummet.

According to Harper's, that record is "reaffirming journalism's essential role in a democratic society." If Maher embodies the essence of American journalism, let alone a democratic society, why do so few people actually want to listen to her brand of journalism?

It is Uri Berliner who deserves this award, not the CEO who hounded him out for seeking greater balance at NPR.

title: Useless Without Transmission: DOE Backs $581 Million TVA Grid Expansion
desc:
Useless Without Transmission: DOE Backs $581 Million TVA Grid Expansion

On the same day we asked how much of the grid’s bill is really AI’s, the Department of Energy offered a partial answer.

@TVAnews and @ENERGY are supporting readily-available, affordable energy that powers Tennessee and the nation. @POTUS is lowering costs for over 2 million families and businesses while bringing new innovation and employment to the Volunteer State to the tune of 800 jobs.

— Senator Bill Hagerty (@SenatorHagerty) October 13, 2026

On Tuesday, DOE said it plans to help the Tennessee Valley Authority fund 84 transmission and distribution projects across eight states to add about 2.5 gigawatts of grid capacity. The award totals roughly $581 million, with $250 million in federal money and $331 million from TVA.

“America’s electric grid cannot become a roadblock to economic growth,” said Katie Jereza, who heads DOE’s Office of Electricity.

Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly went further, blaming “years of misguided energy policies under the previous administration” for leaving the bulk power system “less robust than it should be.”

From $250 Million To $10.5 Billion

The announcement for TVA support from the DOE is alongside the ongoing SPARK program under the GRIP program… If the acronyms are starting to blur together, here is the simple version:

  • Tuesday’s award is for $250 million, written to TVA and its local power companies.
  • SPARK, DOE’s acronym for “Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades,” is the bigger, nationwide program. It puts $1.9 billion of federal money, plus $3.35 billion in cost share, into 31 projects in 26 states that will reconductor or rebuild more than 1,500 miles of existing lines and free up over 23 GW of capacity. TVA’s slice is about $80 million to upgrade roughly 125 miles of lines in Tennessee, Alabama and North Carolina with advanced conductors, adding about 1,900 MW.
  • GRIP, the Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships program, is the even bigger $10.5 billion pot created by the 2021 infrastructure law, and it pays for both SPARK and the new award announced Tuesday afternoon.

Add TVA’s two awards together and it has nearly $741 million in planned grid investment for more than 4,300 MW of added grid capacity.

The Real Bottleneck

As we just covered, the hyperscalers are fighting over how much of the grid’s bill is theirs, with one telling Senate staff that shared upgrades provide a “system benefit which should be shared among all ratepayers.”

Tuesday’s award is that argument in practice, with taxpayers and utility customers splitting the cost of wires everyone uses, on a national grid where, by the senators’ own count, about a third of transmission and half of distribution infrastructure is “near or beyond its useful life.”

You can build all the combined-cycle gas plants, reactors and geothermal wells you want, and line up every data center and electrified factory in the country to buy their output. If the grid can’t carry the power from one to the other, none of it matters.

"there is currently a 3.7-year wait in the US just to get permission to connect to the power grid. Before a single cable is laid or transformer is purchased, AI data centers are stuck in a massive traffic jam." - Goldman it's ok, hyperscalers can just recycle electricity, same way they do revenue

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) August 28, 2026

PJM has already blatantly exposed where the real problem is, as they cried desperately about a need for emergency power. When Constellation showed up with the Three Mile Island reactor restart, PJM told the once-connected nuclear plant to wait patiently for a few years while they set up the connection.

TVA is about to learn that lesson, at scale. Its new long-term plan suggests the region will need 11 to 32 GW of additional generation by 2040. TVA already has 4,120 MW of new capacity under construction, floated as much as 26 GW of new gas in its June draft, and was picked last December for a $400 million DOE award to deploy a newly-licensed GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 small modular reactor at Clinch River.

Every one of those megawatts still needs a way to actually get transported from supply to demand. No amount of new generation fixes a lack of transmission.

Goldman: Power Is “The Primary Risk”

Goldman has been making the same point all year, and it has singled out Tennessee. In May, the commodities team flagged Tennessee as one of the markets “likely to see constrained data center additions since the market is already critically tight.”

In February, the same team told clients that local opposition to data centers was not the real threat: “Ultimately, we believe power tightness remains the primary risk that could slow the US in the AI race with China.” And Goldman now sees behind-the-meter generation powering a quarter of all data centers by 2030.

In other words, a quarter of the industry may simply stop waiting for the grid.

title: Dowd: "Investment Bubbles Are A Feature Of Capitalism, Not A Bug"
desc:
Dowd: "Investment Bubbles Are A Feature Of Capitalism, Not A Bug"

Authored by Ed Dowd via Ed Dowd's Beyond The Narrative Substack,

On Friday October 9th Bloomberg published an article titled "Jeffries' Chris Wood Sees 'Massive Capital Destruction' in AI." His view is that the most likely long-term outcome of the AI boom is massive capital destruction in the US, with market share shifting to cheaper open-source Chinese models. Wood has mostly got it right in my opinion except for two differences. My first difference is that Chinese models are not the only open-source models available and that western open-source models are closing the gap. Secondly, while his view correctly flags the overbuild and the competitive pressure from lower-cost alternatives what it leaves out is the long history of innovative technology infrastructure bubbles and the reliable pattern that follows them which is:

excitement/mania → overinvestment → financial collapse → distressed assets → recapitalized cheap infrastructure fuels the next economic wave.

In regard to the AI bubble, I believe we are currently in the overinvestment phase with cracks emerging. Let us look at some historical examples to illustrate the pattern and see if we can glean what the future of this current bubble might look like.

The US Railroad Bubble

In the decades after the Civil War, railroads became the transformative technology of the era. Capital, much of it European, flooded in. Between the late 1860s and early 1870s, tens of thousands of miles of track were laid, often into sparsely settled or unprofitable territory. Speculative financing, land grants, and the expectation of endless growth created a classic mania. Early projects showed strong returns, which attracted more money into later, riskier lines built far ahead of demand. When financing dried up, highlighted by the failure of Jay Cooke's bank in marketing Northern Pacific bonds, the Panic of 1873 followed. More than 100 railroads went bankrupt in the ensuing years, banks failed, and investors were wiped out. The depression lasted years. Yet the physical tracks remained. The surviving and reorganized network became the backbone of American industrial expansion, enabling efficient movement of goods, people, and capital that powered decades of growth. The overbuilt infrastructure, once distressed and recapitalized, proved far more valuable to the broader economy than the paper losses suggested.

The 1920s Utility Bubble

The 1920s electrification boom followed a similar script. Central-station utilities expanded rapidly, and holding companies consolidated regional systems into large, leveraged empires. Electricity generation and revenues grew dramatically as the technology moved from novelty to infrastructure. Utility stocks soared and became a major part of the market. Holding companies facilitated access to capital and technical expertise, but the structures were opaque, and capacity was built aggressively. The 1929 crash and subsequent Depression exposed the leverage and accounting. Samuel Insull's empire collapsed in spectacular fashion, and the Dow Jones Utilities Average plunged. Reforms including the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 broke up the largest structures and shifted the industry toward regulated regional monopolies. What remained was a vastly expanded electrical grid and generation capacity. Widespread electrification transformed industry, homes, and productivity for the rest of the century. The bust was painful for equity and debt holders; the long-term economic payoff from cheap, abundant power was enormous.

The Dotcom Bubble

The most recent and directly analogous example is the late 1990s telecom fiber buildout during the Dotcom era. Carriers and infrastructure firms poured hundreds of billions into fiber-optic networks, switches, and related equipment, largely financed with debt and encouraged by forecasts of internet traffic doubling every few months. Capacity vastly exceeded near-term demand. After the bubble burst, market values collapsed, many telecoms went bankrupt, and bandwidth prices fell sharply. A large portion of the newly laid fiber sat "dark" or unlit. Through bankruptcies and recapitalizations, that physical infrastructure was acquired at deep discounts, often pennies on the dollar. The resulting cheap broadband made business models viable that would have been prohibitively expensive otherwise. Google, YouTube, Facebook, Apple's smartphone ecosystem, Netflix, software-as-a-service, and cloud services all scaled on that excess capacity. Without the overbuilding and subsequent distress, Web 2.0 as we know it does not happen at the same speed or cost. The capital destruction was real but the residual infrastructure seeded the next wave of growth.

AI Bubble (Yes it is a bubble!)

I believe we are now in the AI infrastructure equivalent of the overinvestment phase. Massive capital is flowing into data centers, chips, power, and related equipment. The sheer scale of spending is turning advanced AI models into a commodity faster than many equity and debt investors appear to appreciate. Chinese open-source models are already applying downward pricing pressure, consistent with the Jefferies view. Cracks are visible. In my Substack piece "Wall Street's AI Capex Party...It's 2 AM & The Bar Is About to Close!", the signals included stalled private credit funding for the buildout, cracking enterprise demand as promised productivity gains fail to materialize at scale, looming power constraints that are becoming the binding limit rather than chip supply, and open-source pricing pressure that compresses margins.

Additional recent indicators from public commentary reinforce this: circular deals in which AI companies run negative free cash flow and rely on debt investors to keep purchasing chips at elevated prices; recent analyses showing major players cannot cover contracted compute commitments under realistic revenue assumptions; and narrative shifts such as space based data centers that paper over terrestrial grid and power bottlenecks. Growth rates implied by current valuations look vulnerable once the second derivative of funding and utilization slows. It is not a question of not if the bubble bursts but when it bursts.

Credit Markets Always End Infrastructure Buildouts

Debt and credit have been central to every one of these infrastructure buildouts. In the railroad boom, bonds financed the majority of the expansion, often more than three-quarters of the capital. When those markets stopped absorbing new bond issues (e.g. Jay Cooke & Co. could no longer place Northern Pacific bonds) the credit system seized up. Then bank runs followed, the New York Stock Exchange closed for ten days, and within two years roughly a third of outstanding railroad bonds had stopped paying interest. The equity markets lagged in this period...credit markets ended the railroad party abruptly.

The 1920s utility expansion followed the same pattern on a different scale. Samuel Insull's holding company pyramid relied on layers of debt and bank loans secured by the securities of the operating companies themselves (financial engineering). Once revenues softened and the banks refused to roll the notes in 1932, the structure collapsed into receivership. In this period the equity markets led the credit markets first with the 1929 crash then credit followed later.

In the telecom fiber boom, carriers raised hundreds of billions in bonds and used vendor financing and circular deals to keep the buildout going. Credit markets ultimately marked the end of the buildout but equities peaked in March of 2000 before credit. Credit spreads later widened sharply in 2001 and 2002, defaults clustered in the sector for years, and bondholders recovered roughly twenty cents on the dollar in many cases. When lenders stopped funding incremental capacity, the overinvestment phase ended and the financial collapse began.

The same dynamic is now visible in the AI buildout, where private credit has stalled, circular debt structures are proliferating, off balance sheet financing is growing and early signs of stress are appearing in CCC junk credit markets. Whether equity markets lead or lag this cycle remains to be seen but the case could be made that given the tremendous amount of passive equity investing the discounting mechanism of equity could lag and credit leads this time.

Bottom Line

Innovative technology capex cycles repeat themselves because human nature has not changed. Mania and excitement give way to overinvestment, which produces financial collapse and distressed assets. Those assets then become the cheap foundation for the next economic wave. Those who believe in cycles and a constant human nature may want to protect themselves accordingly and reduce exposure in the AI complex where risk-reward no longer makes sense. Then when the bust does arrive watch for the opportunities that emerge from the ashes where durable longer-term value will be created.

Bubbles are a feature of capitalism, not a bug. They destroy capital in the short run and, through the process of overbuilding and recapitalization, often leave behind the physical and technical foundation for longer-term productivity gains. The pattern is consistent throughout history...though the timing and severity may vary. The long-term outcome for the economy is usually more favorable than the peak-to-trough equity charts imply and a net positive over time.

"What has been will be again, what has been done will be done again; there is nothing new under the sun." Ecclesiastes 1:9

  • Return on average tangible common equity 12.6% (14.9% adjusted, vs 16% in Q1)
  • Basel III CET1 ratio, advanced approach, 12%, missing estimate of 12.4%
  • Standardized CET1 ratio 10.9%, missing estimate of 11.2%
  • Loans $1.25 trillion, beating estimate of $1.23 trillion
  • Total deposits $2.04 trillion, in line with estimates

Here is how BofA itself presents the quarter, with the "charge impact" row helpfully doing the heavy lifting. Also it's remarkable how quick Bank of America managed to flow through the "surprise" $1.2 billion charge not only through its financial statements but its presentations too just 12 hours later...

Note the bottom box: "Moderated capital markets activity"... followed by "Record year-to-date sales and trading revenue." Both are technically true but only one of them describes Q3.

The Trading Desk That Missed The Party

On Tuesday, JPMorgan and Goldman both stumbled in FICC but more than made up for it in equities: JPM's stock traders brought in $4.95 billion vs a $4.47 billion estimate, while Goldman's equities desk posted $6.44 billion, crushing the $5.09 billion consensus. Citi's bond traders, meanwhile, had their best third quarter in at least a decade according to Bloomberg.

BofA managed to miss on both sides of the desk. FICC revenue ex-DVA tumbled 17% YoY to $2.55 billion, which the bank blamed on "mortgages, municipals, and credit," a far uglier drop than JPM's 4% decline or Goldman's ~1% dip. Equities rose 10% YoY to $2.51 billion, which BofA calls a "record 3Q"... and which still came in $120 million short of what analysts expected.

Sequentially, it looks even worse: total sales and trading revenue ex-DVA dropped 29% from Q2's $7.16 billion to $5.06 billion, with FICC down 28% QoQ and equities down 31%. As a result, Global Markets net income collapsed by $1.4 billion QoQ to $1.2 billion, return on allocated capital plunged from 20% in Q2 to just 9%, and the segment's efficiency ratio blew out to 72% from 56% (chart source BofA).

Which brings us to Goldman's bank earnings preview from Tuesday morning. The bank's desk listed the key question for BAC as "Any NII upside updated for the rate curve and can this flow into operating leverage? Trading outlook relative to peers." We now have the answer to the second part: dead last. And Goldman bank analyst Richard Ramsden, who has a Buy on the stock, made the bull case in his Large Cap Banks preview (available here for pro subs) in part on BofA's lower sensitivity to Wall Street's revenue cycle:

We remain constructive on BAC's NII trajectory through 2026E/27E, and view the high end of the 2026 guidance as achievable with potential upside as well, especially driven by a better NIM outlook. Further, given BAC's asset sensitivity, and less exposure to capital markets revenue risk, we see an increasingly attractive top-line growth story.

Diversification at its finest: the less-exposed business is the one that missed by 6.5%.

Dealmaking: "Pipelines Remain Robust" (Fees, Less So)

Investment banking was the one capital-markets line that technically beat, with fees of $1.80 billion edging out the $1.77 billion estimate thanks to debt underwriting ($958 million vs $920 million expected). But the trend is hardly flattering: total IB fees fell 11% YoY and 16% QoQ, with advisory down 19% from a year ago to $471 million and equity underwriting short of estimates at $395 million. BofA's slide promises that "investment banking pipelines remain robust," which is what every bank says right before the fees fail to show up (chart source BofA).

This fits with Goldman's preview framing of whether Q3 was "just an air pocket or a signal of a more prolonged slowdown to come" as rising yields weigh on deal activity. With the 10Y knocking on 5% and Warsh's Fed eyeing hikes, we know which way we'd lean.

NII Delivers, Expenses Eat It

The good news, and the reason the stock isn't down even more, is net interest income. NII rose 8% YoY to $16.4 billion ($16.6 billion FTE), beating estimates, and the net interest yield jumped 15bps from a year ago to 2.16%, ahead of the 2.11% expected. Rising rates finally work in BofA's favor: the bank estimates a parallel +100bp shift in the curve would add $1.4 billion to NII over the next 12 months, while a -100bp shift would cost it $1.9 billion. Some $2.0 billion of the NII came from Global Markets, up from $1.5 billion a year ago (chart source BofA).

The bad news is the other half of Goldman's question: whether NII upside "can flow into operating leverage." Not this quarter. Total revenue rose $0.9 billion, or 3%, YoY. Adjusted noninterest expense (i.e. excluding the fine) rose $1.2 billion, or 7%, to $18.5 billion, "driven by revenue-related expenses and investments in technology and brand." Costs grew more than twice as fast as revenue, pushing the adjusted efficiency ratio up to 62% from 60% a year ago; including the penalty, it hit 66% (chart source BofA).

Good news for shareholders: compensation expense of $10.97 billion came in slightly below the $11.08 billion estimate. Traders who missed by 6.5% might see it differently (at least the one who aren't replaced by a chatbot).

Capital: Paying Out More Than It Earns

The CET1 miss deserves more attention than it will get. The standardized CET1 ratio fell 37bps QoQ to 10.9%, below the 11.2% estimate, as CET1 capital dropped $3 billion to $198 billion while risk-weighted assets rose $32 billion to $1.82 trillion. Meanwhile, BofA paid $2.2 billion in dividends and repurchased another $6.0 billion of stock, a total of $8.2 billion returned in a quarter when it earned $6.9 billion. The share count is down 5.6% in a year to 6.92 billion, which flatters per-share numbers. That math only works for so long, and Goldman already flagged "less excess capital... and higher rates impacting AOCI" as a reason buybacks could slow at the money centers.

Credit And The Consumer: The One Clean Spot

Asset quality was the bright spot. Provision for credit losses dropped to $1.27 billion, well below the $1.49 billion estimate, while net charge-offs fell to $1.35 billion from $1.41 billion in Q2, below the $1.44 billion expected. BofA released a net $80 million of reserves, and the credit card charge-off rate improved to 3.22%. Commercial reservable criticized exposure dropped to $19.9 billion, with the criticized rate of 2.49% the lowest since 4Q19. One small blemish: consumer loans 30+ days past due rose to $4.58 billion from $4.49 billion a year ago, even as 90+ day delinquencies fell (chart source BofA).

"Asset quality continued to improve and liquidity and capital remained strong," CFO Alastair Borthwick said. The first part is true; see above for the second.

As for the consumer, BofA's spending data still shows a population that is spending, if mostly on things it can't avoid. Combined credit and debit card spend rose 8% YoY to $266 billion, while year-to-date card spending on gas is up 16%, more than double the 7% increase in total spend, courtesy of the Iran war oil shock. That is the same 16% pace the bank flagged for March back in April, so six months later the pain at the pump hasn't eased (chart source BofA).

"We Understand The Seriousness": What Management Said

CEO Brian Moynihan opened the earnings call by addressing the regulatory order before anything else, according to Bloomberg:

"We understand the seriousness of compliance and we are responsible for getting it right. We've invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime. The team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to be addressed by the regulators."

Billions of dollars and thousands of employees, and Treasury still concluded the bank "effectively outsourced" its suspicious-activity detection to law enforcement subpoenas. Not a great return on investment. CFO Alastair Borthwick told reporters the bank had been working with regulators "for some time" on the resolution, per Reuters, which notes that BofA is now under a consent order requiring it to work with a third party to find and report the suspicious transactions that went undetected. Analysts quoted by Reuters flagged the obvious follow-up questions: more expenses, and how long the order lasts.

On the trading miss, the excuses were thinner. Last month BofA told investors it expected Q3 sales and trading revenue to be relatively flat YoY; it came in down 5%. It also guided to an investment banking fee decline of at least 10% because it "wasn't well positioned in some businesses that saw more activity," and delivered -11%. Borthwick's take:

"The environment for deal making remains solid. It's a pretty active environment."

Translation: the party was fine, all right, BofA just wasn't invited. Per Dealogic, the bank slipped to fourth place in the global investment banking league table for the first nine months of 2026, from third a year earlier, and that comes a day after Reuters reported BofA was losing bankers while telling staff about its "big ambition." Or, as Zacks' Brian Mulberry put it to Reuters, "the poor capital markets performance doubles the negative impact of the earnings miss."

Bottom Line

Six months ago, BofA jumped on record equity trading revenue and a higher NII forecast. This quarter, NII once again did its job, but the trading desks missed on both FICC and equities in a quarter when their competitors' stock traders printed money, costs ran more than twice as fast as revenue, and capital ratios slipped below expectations as buybacks outran earnings.

And then there is the fine. Management will spend the 8:30am call talking about the "$1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge," which is a convenient thing to talk about since it is excluded from the adjusted numbers. But the adjusted numbers missed too. As we said last night, the dollar amount was never the real story: the bank that Treasury says "prioritized its revenues" over compliance (a problem it first disclosed back in October 2024) just reported a quarter where the revenues didn't show up either. And with the independent lookback and reviews still ahead, this is unlikely to be the last "one-time" item.

The market's verdict got harsher as the call went on: BAC, down 4.2% premarket, was down 7.2% shortly after the open (not helped by a hot CPI print that revived rate-hike bets), on top of Tuesday's 1.2% drop. That puts the stock around $50, about 23% below its 52-week high of $65.22 and down 8.9% YTD. Goldman's Ramsden still has a Buy on the name. After today, the NII story is the only part of that thesis that is left.

title: CVS To Pay $315 Million Over Claims It Filled Unlawful Opioid Prescriptions
desc:
CVS To Pay $315 Million Over Claims It Filled Unlawful Opioid Prescriptions

Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times,

CVS Pharmacy Inc. and related entities agreed Tuesday to pay $315 million to resolve Justice Department allegations that the company illegally filled opioid and other controlled-substance prescriptions and billed many of them to Medicare and other federal health programs.

The sum settles claims that the company illegally filled such prescriptions from Oct. 17, 2013, through Dec. 2, 2025.

The government alleged CVS knowingly filled prescriptions that lacked a legitimate medical purpose, were not valid, or were not issued in the usual course of professional practice.

Those included dangerous and excessive quantities of opioids, early refills, and "trinity" combinations of an opioid, a benzodiazepine, and a muscle relaxant.

CVS also allegedly filled prescriptions from "pill mill" prescribers while ignoring red flags. Many of these claims were later reimbursed by federal programs.

"Not only does this settlement hold bad actors accountable for their fraudulent activities, but Americans are safer because of it," Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. said in a statement. "Today's settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department's efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances."

According to the complaint, corporate policies kept pharmacists from warning one another about problem prescribers.

Beyond the payment, CVS entered a memorandum of agreement with the DEA.

It requires a hotline for employees and the public to report suspected illegal dispensing, proactive monitoring of pharmacy patterns, and a process to evaluate prescribers suspected of illegal practices.

The settlement agreement says: "The claims asserted against CVS ... are allegations only. There has been no determination of liability."

The settlement also resolves a False Claims Act whistleblower suit filed in 2019 by former CVS employee Hillary Estright of Tennessee. The amount awarded in that case hasn't yet been determined.

CVS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The DOJ unsealed the complaint against CVS in December 2024.

In April 2025, the DOJ announced that Walgreens agreed to pay up to $350 million to settle allegations that it knowingly filled millions of unlawful opioid and other controlled-substance prescriptions and submitted false claims to federal health programs.

The settlement resolved claims that Walgreens violated both the Controlled Substances Act and the False Claims Act from 2012 through 2023.

Individual states have also taken legal action against CVS.

In May 2023, Nevada reached a settlement with CVS Pharmacy worth nearly $152 million over the company's role in the opioid epidemic.

In March 2022, Florida reached more than $878 million in settlements with CVS Health Corp. and three drug companies to resolve claims and avert a trial over their roles in fueling an opioid epidemic in the state. CVS was responsible for $484 million of that total.

CVS Health Corp. is the parent company of CVS Pharmacy.

title: Former Gang Leader Sentenced To 40 Years To Life In Tupac Shakur Murder
desc:
Former Gang Leader Sentenced To 40 Years To Life In Tupac Shakur Murder

Authored by Savannah Hulsey Pointer via The Epoch Times,

A former gang leader was sentenced to 40 years to life in prison on Tuesday for his part in the 1996 death of rapper Tupac Shakur.

Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, faced the potential of life without the possibility of parole after he was convicted of orchestrating the drive-by shooting that killed the hip-hop star.

A five-time convicted felon at the time of Shakur's death, Davis was arrested in 2023 for Shakur's murder and has said on multiple occasions he will appeal his conviction.

Before the sentence was handed down on Oct. 13, prosecutors argued against the minimum sentence, telling Clark County District Court Judge Carli Kierny in Nevada that Shakur's murder was a "uniquely painful situation."

Shakur was shot on Sept. 7, 1996, while in the passenger seat of an SUV driven by record executive Marion "Suge" Knight.

The murder was left unsolved for decades, and despite Davis's conviction, there are still questions about who might have actually pulled the trigger on the shot that killed the 25-year-old rapper.

Authorities long stated they believed Davis was involved in Shakur's killing, but for decades hadn't had enough evidence to take to trial in the previously cold case.

However, Davis went public with his story, including a memoir, recorded conversations, and media appearances, much of which was used against him at trial.

Davis's conviction was for masterminding the attack, which was said to have been in retaliation for Shakur allegedly beating Davis's nephew inside the MGM Grand casino hours earlier on the Las Vegas Strip on Sept. 7, 1996.

Shakur, who lived in Los Angeles, was associated with an area street gang, the Mob Piru, which was also connected to Shakur's music label, Death Row Records.

Davis and his nephew were affiliated with another Los Angeles gang, the South Side Compton Crips, which was known to be a rival gang.

Both groups were in Las Vegas to see a heavyweight boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon on the night of the altercation between Davis's nephew and Shakur.

After the brawl between the men and other individuals known to be part of both gangs, Davis, his nephew, and two others took a vehicle to look for Shakur and Knight to settle the score, according to court records.

Davis has maintained that one of the others in the vehicle shot into the car carrying Knight and Shakur while in traffic.

Shakur's half-sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, spoke about the impact of her brother's death, saying he was "born an icon." She recalled her brother's care toward her and her siblings, calling him the "father figure" in their home.

Sekyiwa Shakur said her brother was paying the bills and buying food for 17 different families at the time of his death. She said her brother's death "for a long time, crippled" many of those in her family, especially those in the car procession who saw the shooting.

In her tearful description of her brother, she said he put his life on the line, fed those who were hungry, and was "gentle and kind to women and children."

She went on, saying, "I do believe that when you take a life like that, you deserve every minute ... of the maximum amount of punishment, time to sit down and contemplate what you've done to this world."

While authorities never accused Davis of actually pulling the trigger, Nevada law allows participants in a crime to be charged with murder.

The jury deliberated for three hours before handing down the guilty verdict.

The actual shooter was never identified by law enforcement, and all three other men in the vehicle with Davis on the night of Shakur's death have since died.

The rapper was struck by four bullets and died in the hospital six days later. Knight suffered only minor injuries and is currently serving a 28-year prison sentence for an unrelated voluntary manslaughter conviction.

Davis acknowledged in his book, "Compton Street Legend," that he was a suspect in the murders of Shakur and rival rapper Christopher Wallace.

Wallace, who was known as the Notorious B.I.G., with New York-based Bad Boy Entertainment, was killed in Los Angeles in a March 1997 shooting long suspected to be in retaliation for Shakur's killing.

Wallace's murder is still unsolved.

title: Can Lasers Beat Drone Swarms? The Pentagon Is About To Find Out
desc:
Can Lasers Beat Drone Swarms? The Pentagon Is About To Find Out

Authored by Alex Kimani via OilPrice,

The enormous expansion of drone warfare is forcing militaries to reconsider how much ammunition they can afford to fire at relatively cheap targets. The Pentagon is betting that some of that ammunition can be replaced with electricity, selecting four directed-energy systems for operational testing at five U.S. military bases.

The Pentagon selected AeroVironment's (NASDAQ: AVAV) Palletized High-Energy Laser, Boeing's (NYSE: BA) Compact Laser Weapon System, Kord Technologies' Firefly high-energy laser and Epirus' Leonidas high-powered microwave. The three lasers concentrate energy on individual targets, while Leonidas uses microwave energy to disable electronics and can engage multiple drones.

Fort Bliss in Texas, Naval Base Kitsap in Washington, Fort Huachuca in Arizona, Grand Forks Air Force Base in North Dakota and Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri will host the weapons. Congress mandated the five-base pilot earlier this year, with deployments scheduled to begin later in 2026.

The four weapons will operate at the five bases for a full year, giving the Pentagon its first sustained look at how directed-energy systems hold up outside short military demonstrations. More systems will get their chance in December, when Joint Interagency Task Force 401 stages a directed-energy "shoot-off" at Utah's Dugway Proving Ground, with the Pentagon prepared to buy weapons that perform well.

"High-energy lasers and high-powered microwave systems are tools that can be effectively used in a layered drone defense," Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF-401, said in announcing the selections. "This pilot program will test these capabilities in an operational environment so we can understand how best to integrate and sustain them to defend the homeland."

The Pentagon is already committing billions of dollars to counter-drone defenses, with JIATF-401 awarding 10 contracts worth up to $4.15 billion in September under a wider procurement vehicle with a ceiling of $7 billion.

The cost difference can run into millions of dollars per engagement. According to the Government Accountability Office, firing a directed-energy weapon costs approximately $1 to $10 in fuel for electricity generation and cooling, compared with $4.1 million for a Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptor in fiscal 2023. The Patriot can engage more sophisticated threats, including ballistic and cruise missiles, but using conventional interceptors against inexpensive drones creates an enormous cost disadvantage. Lasers and microwave weapons eliminate the need to replace ammunition after every engagement, although their effectiveness depends on available power, cooling, range and operating conditions.

Boeing has already put its Compact Laser Weapon System against Group 3 drones, destroying three during the Red Sands exercise in Saudi Arabia in 2024. The system used just 5 kilowatts of power and was plugged into the Army's existing Forward Area Air Defense network, taking its targeting data from an external radar. Five kilowatts means keeping the beam on a drone longer than with more powerful lasers, but Boeing gets something in return: a smaller weapon that can be moved and deployed much more easily.

Epirus' Leonidas uses high-powered microwave pulses to disable the electronics inside multiple drones at once, giving it a potential role against swarms. The company has also demonstrated Leonidas against fiber-optic-guided FPV drones, which maintain a physical connection to their operators instead of depending on the radio links targeted by conventional electronic jamming.

Ukraine is already putting the same economics to work against Russian drones, turning electricity into a 50-cent alternative to conventional air-defense ammunition. Ukrainian developers have built and tested Sunray and Tryzub, with a Sunray node costing roughly $300,000 to manufacture. Ukraine wants hundreds of the smaller laser systems mounted on vehicles and rooftops rather than a limited number of large installations. At 50 cents per shot, thousands of laser engagements would still cost less in ammunition than a single conventional air-defense missile.

title: Judge Extends Order Allowing News Agencies White House Access
desc:
Judge Extends Order Allowing News Agencies White House Access

Authored by Stacy Robinson via The Epoch Times,

A federal judge has extended his order forbidding President Donald Trump from excluding certain media outlets from accessing the White House.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a memorandum opinion on Oct. 13 granting a preliminary injunction sought by CNN, MS NOW, and Politico to maintain the block on the president's press ban, finding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their First Amendment discrimination claim.

Trump announced on social media last month that he was banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico "as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

After the outlets sued, Kelly ordered the White House to temporarily restore access on Sept. 24, ruling that the government likely violated their Fifth Amendment due process rights by abruptly taking away their press passes without notice or a hearing.

Attorney Theodore J. Boutrous Jr. told the court at an Oct. 8 hearing that Trump wanted to ban the outlets because of their viewpoints.

"He doesn't like scrutiny of his policies, he doesn't like the reporting, he wants more good press," he said.

Department of Justice Senior Counsel Michael Velchik pushed back, telling the court that Trump was more concerned with media outlets allegedly fabricating quotes, splicing together interviews, and using anonymous sources.

"He doesn't mind negative press stories if he deserves them. He has problems with trafficking verifiable falsehoods," he said.

The government argued it was necessary to exclude those outlets in the name of national security and to prevent leaks of classified information.

But Kelly said, when originally ordering the White House to restore access, that there was no evidence on the record to back up that claim.

In his ruling on Tuesday, Kelly said Trump likely revoked their access to the White House press area "because he believes their coverage of him and his administration is generally inaccurate and biased," rather than for legitimate government interests such as maintaining professional standards for journalists or protecting national security.

"Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination," the judge wrote.

Kelly also said the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in their claim that the administration denied them due process rights under the Fifth Amendment by revoking their access without prior notice.

The judge determined that the administration's letters outlining the reasons for the hard passes revocation were inadequate because the outlets received the letters only after the ban was implemented.

The letters cited reports that the administration said "threatened national security and spread falsehoods," including coverage of "'top-secret' construction details" about the East Wing bunker and funding for the White House ballroom.

The White House said the reports included detailed descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements, according to the government's Sept. 22 court filing.

The judge said there was no evidence that Trump had relied on the reported incidents cited in the letters when deciding to revoke the outlets' hard passes.

The Epoch Times reached out to the White House for comment but did not receive a response by publication time.

Trump signaled on Sept. 21 that he expected the judge to rule in favor of the outlets and said his administration would appeal if that happened.

"In any event, I have an obligation to fight for the Success and Safety of our Country. FAKE NEWS IS A THREAT TO DEMOCRACY, and I will do whatever is necessary to make sure that the U.S.A. thrives," he wrote in a Truth Social post.

title: Cornell Bans Fraternity Parties Amid Gang Rape Allegations
desc:
Cornell Bans Fraternity Parties Amid Gang Rape Allegations

Authored by Jackson Richman via The Epoch Times,

Cornell University has banned parties at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid a reopened investigation into an alleged rape on campus two years ago.

In an Oct. 13 statement, the university's president, Michael Kotlikoff, said "all parties and social events in Interfraternity Council (IFC) houses at Cornell will be suspended for the remainder of the 2026 - 2027 academic year." This, he said, gives "time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue."

Fraternities that hold in-house parties or events would be subject to an immediate emergency suspension.

Cornell has more than 20 active fraternities affiliated with its IFC. The Epoch Times has reached out to the IFC for comment.

It is unclear whether the new policy applies to off-campus gatherings and events.

Kotlikoff's statement comes less than two weeks after New York Attorney General Letitia James announced an investigation into an alleged gang rape of a woman by Cornell students in October 2024.

That woman, a Cornell student only known as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit on Sept. 16 against the university, the Chi Phi fraternity, and others, alleging sexual assault and negligence. Cornell said that an internal probe led to some students being expelled, other students being suspended, and Chi Phi being kicked off campus. No students were criminally charged.

The woman was "plied with alcohol and drugs to the point of intoxication" at a fraternity house in Ithaca, New York, in October 2024, according to the lawsuit. She was "incapable of consenting" when coerced into taking drugs and forced to participate in sexual acts, the lawsuit stated. She reported the incident to campus police in November 2024.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation into the alleged rape after the suit was filed. The woman went to campus police but did not claim she was gang raped or drugged, he said in a statement on Sept. 28. Instead, she "described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

"Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence," Van Houten said at the time. "I have been asked by the community to revisit the decision whether to pursue criminal charges against the seven fraternity members. I have already begun that process, starting with our conversation with Jane Doe and her attorneys."

Cornell welcomed the renewed investigation into what allegedly happened. Kotlikoff said the Ivy League school would carry out reforms in response.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor to probe what occurred, removing Van Houten from the case.

The woman went to police and alleged she was raped, according to the governor during an Oct. 2 briefing.

"Yet, shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors," Hochul said.

Van Houten supported the move and said he would cooperate with James.

"I support the appointment of Attorney General James and I trust that she will examine the facts and apply the law," he previously said in a statement to The Epoch Times.

Cornell has hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent review of the school's response.

In his statement, Kotlikoff said there would be more staff to the Cornell Office of Civil Rights, "including the appointment of a dedicated case manager who will help individuals who report sexual misconduct navigate other university processes as needed."

He also said Cornell is working with the New York State Police to allow their criminal investigators, who are independent of the school, to investigate allegations of sexual assault on the campus.

Cornell will "accelerate the implementation of the recommendations of the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault and expand the scope and nature of the recommendations by engaging the campus community," according to Kotlikoff.

"These are first steps toward systemic change on our campus," he said. "We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe's experiences, and those of other survivors.

"Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question."

Kotlikoff's statement comes ahead of a faculty senate meeting where members are expected to vote on a measure expressing no confidence in the administration on its handling of sexual assault at the university.

title: The problem with living in a rich man’s world | Letters
desc:
David Redshaw and Fernando Quintana respond to reports of a billionaire exodus from Britain

The idea that the departure of the super-rich is a problem ignores a historical fact (Apparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playground, 7 October). Capitalism works better without them. The most successful countries today are states where redistributive taxation has empowered the working masses and provided a better and more stable market for business people.

How do today’s complaining uber-rich explain the postwar decades, when the top rate of income tax was commonly 80% or 90%, and yet the period is known as a golden age of capitalism? Then Margaret Thatcher lowered the top rate to 60% and the country tilted into a massive recession. The rich get to a point where they simply become wealth extractors, using their money to buy assets and raising the cost of them for the rest of us – housing being a good example today.
